course.title: Discrete Mathematics and Logic for Computing
course.tagline: Test a claim in code, then prove it: sets, relations, logic, induction, counting and graphs, applied to joins, rules, collisions, re-identification and pipelines
course.description: Participants practise the discrete mathematics and proof that computing degrees assume: sets, relations, logic, proof, counting and graphs. Code tests each claim on generated cases before it is proved, so the gap between testing and proof is visible. Labs link relations to joins, logic to rule checking, counting to collision and re-identification risk, and graphs to pipeline dependencies. Algorithms on graphs follow in FND-PRG-103.
course.audience: Beginners. Career changers and non-computing graduates closing bridging gaps before advanced study, and computing graduates refreshing the mathematics behind models; a placement test lets participants skip any course whose content they already command.
prerequisites: Writes short Python programs with lists, loops, functions and recursion (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)
course.format_note: Extended: 7 weeks part-time, one session and one lab a week, weekly graded problem sets and a capstone portfolio

outcomes.text: Identify whether a relation is a function, an equivalence or an order, and which properties it has, given twelve relations from data and software
outcomes.evidence: supervised AI-off test, at least 70% correct

outcomes.text: Distinguish valid from invalid arguments and translate plain-language rules into propositional and predicate logic, given five access and data-quality rules
outcomes.evidence: rules checked by truth table or solver, four of five correct

outcomes.text: Describe direct, contradiction and induction proofs and identify the gap in a flawed proof, given six short proofs, two with planted errors
outcomes.evidence: marked answers in the supervised test

outcomes.text: Apply induction and loop invariants to prove simple claims about integers, sets and recursive code, given claims first tested in code
outcomes.evidence: rubric-marked proofs, each with its test code

outcomes.text: Compute counts of arrangements, selections and collisions and verify them by enumeration, given hashing and record-linkage problems
outcomes.evidence: a notebook in which formula and brute-force counts agree

outcomes.text: Use a graph model of dependencies to find cycles and compute a topological order, given a pipeline graph with a planted cycle
outcomes.evidence: output naming the cycle and a valid order once it is removed

case_study.name: The community volunteer centre (fictional)
case_study.summary: An unnamed non-profit in one unnamed city registers 4,000 volunteers, trains them and staffs community events in twelve postal districts; its analyst checks joins, access rules, a shift schedule, check-in codes, a de-identified extract and a nightly pipeline. All data is synthetic, generated with a fixed seed; people appear only as codes such as V-00412, never by name.

Compose two relations and explain how a database join differs from the composition

days.label: Capstone
days.title: Portfolio oral defences
days.subtitle: Ten minutes each: one proof the assessor selects, explained step by step, then a changed hypothesis

capstone.summary: A portfolio of three proofs, at least one by induction, each preceded by test code, with a ten-minute oral defence of one proof the assessor selects
capstone.submission: A link to a public GitHub repository holding the portfolio: three proofs, at least one by induction, each preceded by its test code and that code's output, with a record of any AI use; then a ten-minute oral defence of one proof the assessor selects, explained step by step, with a changed hypothesis to handle

rubric.criterion: Each claim stated precisely: domain, quantifiers, hypothesis and conclusion
Test code before each proof: generated or exhaustive cases, edge cases, and an honest note of what the tests cannot show
Each proof valid: method named, every step justified, no gap
The induction proof complete: base case, hypothesis stated, an inductive step that uses it (or an invariant with initialisation, maintenance and termination)
Portfolio readable and reproducible: code runs, AI use recorded, sources named
